questions.q: In $f(x,y) = (x\cdot y + \sin x)\cdot e^{-y}$ the input $x$ feeds two operations. With upstream gradient $\bar c = \partial f/\partial(xy + \sin x) = e^{-y}$, what does reverse mode store in $x$'s gradient?
options: $(y + \cos x)\,e^{-y}$ — the sum of both messages
$y\cos x\,e^{-y}$ — the product of both messages
questions.explain: Each path from the output to $x$ contributes local × upstream, and the multivariable chain rule *adds* contributions: $y\,e^{-y} + \cos x\,e^{-y}$. Overwriting instead of accumulating keeps only one path — the bug the lab's toggle demonstrates.

questions.q: A network has one scalar loss and $10^8$ parameters. Why is training done with reverse mode rather than forward mode?
options: Forward mode gives only approximate derivatives
Reverse mode gets all $10^8$ partial derivatives from one backward pass; forward mode needs one pass per input
Forward mode cannot handle nonlinear functions like $\sigma$
questions.explain: Both modes are exact. Forward mode propagates one tangent (one input direction) per pass, so it needs $n$ passes for $n$ inputs; reverse mode propagates from the single output and gets every $\partial L/\partial w$ at once — at the price of storing activations.

questions.q: Using dual numbers ($\varepsilon^2 = 0$), evaluate $g(x) = x\cdot x\cdot x$ at $3 + 1\cdot\varepsilon$. What is the result?
questions.explain: $(3+\varepsilon)^3 = 27 + 3\cdot 9\,\varepsilon$ (all higher powers of $\varepsilon$ vanish), and the $\varepsilon$-part $27 = 3x^2$ is exactly $g'(3)$. $9 + 6\varepsilon$ is $(3+\varepsilon)^2$.

questions.q: Why does training a deep network need much more memory than just running it (inference)?
options: Gradients are stored with higher precision
The backward pass needs the forward-pass activations (e.g. $\sigma$'s output for $s(1-s)$), so every layer's values must be kept
Reverse mode has to enumerate every path through the graph
The computational graph must be compiled twice
questions.explain: Local derivatives depend on forward values (the 'saved for backward' column), so activations are kept until the backward pass uses them. Reverse mode never enumerates paths — it shares common prefixes. Gradient checkpointing trades recomputation for this memory.
